title: Panthers’ last-second field goal gives them ugly win over Saints and lead in NFC South
content:
NEW ORLEANS — The Carolina Panthers did everything they could Sunday. They committed a staggering 17 penalties for 152 yards to give the New Orleans Saints one opportunity after another to win the NFC South matchup.

But it was a New Orleans penalty that ended up being the difference maker.

Bryce Young’s deep pass to Jalen Coker fell incomplete but Kool-Aid McKinstry was called for pass interference at the Saints’ 36-yard line with 28 seconds remaining. Moments later, Ryan Fitzgerald hit a 54-yard field goal as time expired to give the Panthers a 20-17 victory.

Fitzgerald had missed a 48-yard attempt in the first quarter, but bounced back with a 55-yarder in the third quarter and then the game-winner. He’ll share the game ball with Chuba Hubbard. The Panthers running back ran for 92 yards and two touchdowns and caught a team-high five passes for a team-best 80 yards. His versatility was on display most when he accounted for all 68 yards and touched the ball on all six plays of the Panthers’ scoring drive that gave them a 17-14 lead late in the fourth quarter.

Hubbard caught a pair of short passes out of the backfield on the drive and turned them into gains of 29 and 33 yards. He topped off that drive with a 1-yard TD run.

“It’s Chuba breaking tackles on checkdowns, in the run game making critical plays because he wants it,” Panthers coach Dave Canales said after the game. “That’s the type of mentality it’s going to take for us to get to where we want to. A full group with that type of mentality and I just love that he’s one of our leaders. He wanted this one bad. You could tell that. You could see by the way he played.”

A mostly ho-hum game turned into a frantic back and forth in the fourth quarter.

New Orleans (3-6) took advantage of four Panthers penalties on a nine-play, 70-yard touchdown drive that ended with a 4-yard Tyler Shough to Alvin Kamara TD pass to pull ahead 14-10 with 3 minutes 49 seconds left in the game. A horse-collar penalty on a Jaelan Phillips sack and a pass interference call on Tre’von Moehrig assisted the Saints on the drive.

After the Panthers responded with Hubbard’s TD, Saints kicker Charlie Smyth hit a 55-yard field goal with 41 seconds left to tie the game, 17-17.

The Panthers (4-5) are now in sole possession of first place in the NFC South with the victory. Canales and his staff will celebrate the win, but will have a lot to work on before their Week 11 matchup against the Ravens after their penalty-filled performance.

Young threw for 200 yards, but didn’t have a TD pass for the first time this season. Shough finished with 187 passing yards with a TD and interception. Kamara scored both of the Saints’ touchdowns on a 3-yard run and 4-yard pass.

For just the second time since the NFL’s realignment in 2002, the NFC South did not have a team with more than three wins entering Week 10. But someone has to win this division, which the Panthers did last year with a losing record (8-9). Carolina put itself in good position to do so again by snapping a three-game losing streak to take sole possession of first place at 4-5. The Panthers also ended a three-game skid at the Superdome, overcoming team records in penalties and penalty yardage and a crazy disparity in accepted penalties (17 to 3).

Dave Canales had a simple charge for Todd Wash when he named the defensive line coach his interim defensive coordinator: Stop the run. In his initial meeting after the promotion, Wash told players they were going to bring a safety into the box and dare opposing backs to beat them. It hasn’t happened yet. After allowing 82 yards on the ground in a loss to Denver last week, the Panthers completely suffocated the Saints’ rushing attack, which came in ranked 23rd. The Saints managed just 49 rushing yards on 23 attempts — 2.1 yards per carry.

The NFL’s most-penalized teams again hurt itself by drawing a barrage of flags. It seems like the Panthers set dubious franchise records for penalties every week, and Sunday was no different. Carolina tied its franchise mark with 17 penalties and set their team record with 152 penalty yards. The Panthers’ penchant for penalties was never more apparent than on the Saints’ go-ahead touchdown drive in the fourth quarter, when they were flagged four times, including a pass interference call against safety Tre’von Moehrig.
